I would keep this year simple and steady. In Quzhou County, the most familiar and reliable pattern for me is winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. At 63, I would not spread myself across too many crops, because that raises labor needs, management difficulty, and risk. I would stay with the wheat-maize rotation because I know how to manage it, it fits local weather and irrigation conditions, and it gives me grain in both seasons.

For the winter wheat already in the ground, I would focus on keeping the stand even, giving enough water at the key stages, and not overdoing inputs. I would use improved seed rather than something fancy, because I want stable performance more than chasing the highest possible yield. I would put most fertilizer in nitrogen, with moderate phosphorus and some potassium, then irrigate at the stages that matter most for wheat growth. I would only spray when needed for the main diseases and pests, because every extra pass costs money.

After wheat harvest, I would plant summer maize on the same area. I would use hybrid maize because in my place that is the safer choice for yield. I would keep the field work lighter after wheat harvest and go with no-tillage for maize to save time and hold soil moisture. I would still feed the crop well, but I would manage fertilizer and water carefully because maize can use inputs quickly in summer. My goal would not be the most aggressive plan. I would choose the plan I can carry through properly from start to finish.
